problem: Language-driven robots need to integrate perception, semantic mapping, LLM reasoning and safe low-level control. Store locations in a corridor shopping task are not given as coordinates, only as junction signboard cues, so the robot must explore and decide from those cues.
motivation: Mobile robots should follow high-level instructions rather than fixed waypoints. End-to-end learned navigation is hard to debug and less safe, so the authors want a modular stack where the LLM makes only discrete semantic decisions and deterministic ROS controllers do the motion.
key_idea: Use an LLM as a constrained discrete decision layer (<direction>|||<store_action>) over an online text/JSON junction-to-POI semantic map and a history log, while a finite-state MainController gates classical motion primitives (wall avoidance, AprilTag approach, store entry, grasping).
insight: Separating semantic decisions (LLM) from deterministic low-level skills makes the system modular and debuggable, since policy logic can change without touching controllers, and the JSON map and history log make decisions inspectable. The paper offers only qualitative evidence, with no ablations or quantitative results. It reports failures from AprilTag loss during approach and from crowded objects during grasping.
method: Signboard/AprilTag perception: a YOLO11-small detector, distilled with pseudo-labels from Qwen2.5-VL, detects arrows, store icons, the pickup point, AprilTags and grasp objects. Each signboard observation becomes a junction record.
Semantic map: a JSON list of junctions, each with direction-POI strings and an estimated (x, y, yaw) pose from ORB-SLAM3 odometry. It separates symbolic from metric knowledge.
History logging: a node logs visited junctions, directions taken and store instances entered to a JSON file that the LLM uses to avoid revisits and track progress.
Order parsing: an LLM constrained by a JSON schema turns the natural-language order into four non-negative counts (hamburger, iced coffee, hot coffee, medicine), with sanity checks.

LLM navigation policy (DecisionMakers): given the map, current junction, remaining order and history, the LLM outputs <dir in {1,2,3}>|||<act in {1..5}>. The output is validated, and the LLM never produces velocity commands.

MainController FSM: latched gating states (WallAvoid, TagApproach, Map, WaitAction, PreEnter, EnterStore, Grasp, Pickup) let only one skill command /cmd_vel. It falls back to wall avoidance on failure or timeout.
Motion primitives: local-costmap wall avoidance (Forward/Turn90/Turn180), gated AprilTag approach with a final forward advance, pre-enter centering, store entry, and a predefined grasp sequence.

setting.backbone: Unspecified LLM (navigation policy and order parsing, frozen prompting); YOLO11-small detector distilled from Qwen2.5-VL; classical ROS controllers
setting.training_data: Custom YOLO dataset of 36,329 images (28,875 train / 7,454 val) from sim and real runs, with Qwen2.5-VL pseudo-labels. The LLM is used zero-shot via prompting.
setting.observation: RGB USB camera (signboards, store-entry centering) + RealSense RGB-D (local costmap, AprilTags, grasp tracking), ORB-SLAM3 pose/odometry
setting.action_space: High-level discrete <direction>|||<store_action> executed by ROS velocity-command motion primitives
setting.privileged: none (store locations not given; AprilTags/signboards are environment anchors)

numbers_note: No quantitative results; only qualitative demonstrations in Gazebo and a real corridor layout.
results: Qualitatively, the integrated stack completed multi-store missions from natural-language instruction to object retrieval and return to the pickup area, in both Gazebo and a real corridor layout. No metrics or baselines are reported. The observed failures were AprilTag loss near entrances and unstable grasps with crowded objects.
limitations: No quantitative evaluation, baselines or ablations; only qualitative demos in one small environment
AprilTag loss during approach causes aborted or inaccurate approaches
Predefined grasp motion is brittle with tightly spaced objects; the environment is heavily engineered (signboards, tags), with the LLM model unspecified
